reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.caveat: THE LOOKUP IS ON NEITHER SIDE — ours holds the slot, the floor holds the object, both resolved outside the clock. That is the comparison this row is for. What ours does that a store cannot: it walks the patch, refuses names a row may not carry, gates each column on the default equality, builds the list of what moved, stamps the slot and the collection, and tests the row's column store and the population's listener list so a column subscriber or an index could be told. THAT DEFAULT IS SAMEVALUEZERO AND WAS AN INLINE `===` WHEN 2026-08-20-price/write WAS RECORDED. The call was there under both — the predicate has always been reached through the strategy's captured parameter — so the delta is one comparison, and only on a column that moved, which is one per write here. `update.column-vs-the-strict-equality-default` is that delta on its own and is unrun; until it runs, this row's recorded figure is a figure for the older body. Direction: inflates our ratio; the tracked row below prices the part of that a person would have had to write anyway. The patch object is REUSED rather than written as a literal per call — a caller who writes { title } inline pays one more allocation per write than this row charges us for. The batch closes with one flush per eight thousand writes, which is why every write in it takes the marking path rather than the already-stamped early return. THE REUSED PATCH IS ALSO WHAT STOPS THIS ROW BEING SUBTRACTED FROM `update.unchanged-vs-field-store`, and that subtraction is the only way anyone has to split this number into the walk that decides and the tail that reports. The unchanged row hands `updateEntity` a DIFFERENT patch object per write and its floor reads the value out of that object; this row reuses one patch and its floor reads a local. Two differences, both on the wrong side of the subtraction. `update.column-vs-field-store-a-patch-per-write` is this row with the unchanged row's patch supply and the unchanged row's floor, and it exists so the split can be taken arm for arm instead of across two bodies that differ in three ways.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — one column, one patch object per row
reading.caveat: THE ROW ABOVE, ARM FOR ARM WITH `update.unchanged-vs-field-store`, AND THAT IS ITS WHOLE REASON. The only handle anybody has on how the row above's gap divides is the unchanged row, which times the same call up to the point where the comparator finds every column equal and returns before marking anything. Subtracting one from the other would give the walk and the tail — except that the two bodies differ in three ways at once: the row above REUSES one patch object where the unchanged row allocates eight thousand and hands a different one to every write, and its floor stores a local where the unchanged row's floor reads the value off the patch first. A fresh patch per write is a fresh receiver for `isPlain` and for the `for…in`, and the extra load is a real instruction on the floor. Both differences push the same way and neither is the thing being priced. THIS ROW REMOVES ALL THREE. The patch supply is the unchanged row's — one object per row, built outside the clock — and the floor is the unchanged row's floor to the character. What is left between this row's `ours` and the unchanged row's `ours` is exactly what a write that MOVES a column does and a write that moves nothing does not: one store into the entity, the moved-names array and its push, two `channel.write` calls — the row and the population — one `columnSlotStoreService.get` probe for the moved column inside `OIMColumnOwner.markColumnsChanged`, and the frame that closes the batch. EIGHT PATCH ARRAYS, ONE PER TITLE, so this row moves the column on exactly the writes the row above moves it on. The title advances by one of eight per batch and every row in a batch is written with the same title, which is the row above's rotation with the shared object unpicked into one object per row. THE FLUSH IS ON THIS SIDE OF THE SUBTRACTION AND NOT ON THE UNCHANGED ROW'S: nothing is marked there, so no frame is asked for. `flush.empty-vs-noop` [2026-08-20-price/frame] prices a frame with nothing queued, and over eight thousand writes it is four thousandths of a nanosecond each — named here because it belongs to the difference, not because it can be seen in it.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.floor: test the row for a column store and the population for listeners, then row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE TWO "IS ANYBODY LISTENING" GUARDS, PUT ON THE FLOOR. A write that moves a column asks two questions before it can skip the routing: `OIMColumnOwner.markColumnsChanged` tests `carrierSlot.columnSlotStore === undefined` (no column of this row was ever subscribed to), and `OIMSlotAggregate.contentChanged` tests `listeners.length === 0` (no index hears this population). Both hold on every row of this fixture. Inside `update.column-vs-field-store` they are two operations among thirty and nothing separates them; here the floor makes the identical two tests on an identically empty state, so THE ITEM IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THAT ROW'S GAP AND THIS ROW'S GAP. OUR ARM IS THAT ROW'S ARM TO THE CHARACTER — the same fixture, the same reused patch, the same rotation of eight titles, the same flush per eight thousand writes. OPERATION COUNT, THE DIFFERENCE ONLY: one field load and one `undefined` compare per row, one length load and one compare per row. Expected inside the noise floor.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.floor: gate on !==, store, then queue the entity once per frame by a stamp kept per position
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR NOW DOES THE JOB. It compares before it writes, so a re-send moves nothing; it keeps a frame stamp per entity position so ten writes to one entity queue it once; and it queues the entity so a frame could deliver it. Four lines. What it still does not do: record WHICH columns moved (so no field-granular subscription is possible), route to an index, or mark the collection separately from the entity. Direction: still inflates our ratio, and this is the number to quote when somebody asks what the engine costs over doing it properly by hand.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntityColumn(slot, 'title', value) — one column, no index reads it
reading.floor: gate on !==, store, then queue the entity once per frame by a stamp kept per position
reading.caveat: The same floor as update.column-vs-tracked-store, against the column door: no patch object and no walk over it. Both sides hand over one value per write and queue each entity at most once per frame.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) with the value the row already holds
reading.floor: row.title = value — a store that always happens
reading.caveat: THE TWO SIDES DO OPPOSITE THINGS, ON PURPOSE. Ours walks the patch, finds every column equal, returns before marking anything and wakes nobody; the floor stores unconditionally because it has nothing to protect. So this is not "which is faster at the same work" — it is what the comparator gate costs when it fires, against the cheapest possible thing that ignores the question. No flush closes this batch, because nothing was marked and there is nothing for a frame to deliver: that is the point of the row. Direction: inflates our ratio; what the gate buys is that a screen re-sending a server payload it already holds does not repaint.

reading.floor: const row = map.get(id); if (row !== undefined) row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE ONE WRITE ROW WHERE BOTH SIDES PAY THE LOOKUP, which is what makes it the fair comparison for a key that arrived from outside. Ours is one map read and then the identity path priced two rows up; the floor is one map read and a store. The difference between this ratio and the update.column ratio is the price of NOT having held the identity — the engine's own source puts that at 103-132 ns against 36-51 [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE], and this row is the independent check on that claim.
